claims.text: Low hardness and strength in equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by intrinsically low lattice-friction stress.
Low lattice friction promotes facile dislocation glide on multiple slip systems.
The alloy lacks strong short-range ordering and precipitates in its starting state.
The absence of short-range order and precipitates allows dislocations to nucleate and move with minimal hindrance.
Minimally hindered dislocation motion produces low work hardening.
The initial CoCrFeNiTi material is a homogeneous single-phase solid solution, likely FCC.
The initial material contains no secondary phases or significant chemical ordering.
The homogeneous solid-solution lattice lacks significant lattice distortion.
Easy dislocation nucleation and glide limit dislocation accumulation and forest strengthening.
Widespread dislocation motion without substantial work hardening causes high ductility together with relatively low hardness and strength.
The as-cast single-phase state will exhibit low yield stress and modest hardness.
After deformation, the starting state will show uniformly distributed dislocation lines with little twinning or dense dislocation entanglement.
Heat treatments that induce precipitates or short-range ordering will increase hardness and strength relative to the starting state.
Chemical ordering can become favorable at lower temperatures in compositionally complex alloys.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply if composition or heat treatment produces precipitation, phase separation, or ordering that changes dislocation interactions.
The relative contributions of lattice friction, solute-dislocation interactions, and incipient chemical ordering have not been quantitatively established.
Slight changes in Ti content may alter local ordering tendencies.
A comparison between homogenized samples and heat-treated samples can test whether obstacle formation raises strength and changes dislocation behavior.
Similar strength, hardness, and dislocation interactions in the two states, or substantial barriers already present in the starting state, would falsify the proposed explanation.
